topics.title: Introduction to Java
topics.description: Understand what Java is, why it became widely used, how Java applications are built, and the characteristics that distinguish Java from lower-level and platform-specific programming languages.

sections.title: What is Java?
sections.content:
Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed to be portable across different computing platforms. Java source code is compiled into bytecode, which can be executed by a Java Virtual Machine (JVM). This execution model allows the same compiled application to run on different operating systems that provide a compatible JVM.

Java is commonly used for backend services, enterprise applications, web applications, distributed systems, desktop applications, and many other types of software. Its standard library and ecosystem provide APIs for collections, networking, file handling, concurrency, database access, security, and other common programming tasks.

sections.title: Why Java is platform-independent
sections.content:
Java achieves platform independence by separating compilation from operating-system-specific execution. The Java compiler converts source code into bytecode rather than directly generating machine instructions for a particular operating system.

The resulting bytecode can be executed by a compatible JVM on Windows, Linux, macOS, or another supported platform. The JVM implementation is platform-specific, but the Java bytecode and application code can remain the same.

This is commonly summarized as "Write Once, Run Anywhere."

sections.title: Main features of Java
sections.content:
Java provides several characteristics that have contributed to its long-term adoption. It supports object-oriented programming, strong static typing, automatic memory management, exception handling, multithreading and concurrency APIs, networking, security mechanisms, and a large standard library.

Java is also designed around a managed runtime. Developers generally do not manually allocate and release object memory in the same way they would in languages such as C. The JVM manages object memory and uses garbage collection to reclaim memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable.

topics.shortDescription: Learn what Java is, how its execution model provides portability, and the core characteristics of the language.

topics.title: JDK, JRE and JVM
topics.description: Understand the roles of the Java Development Kit, Java Runtime Environment, and Java Virtual Machine, and how they work together when developing and running Java applications.

sections.title: What is JVM?
sections.content:
JVM stands for Java Virtual Machine. It is the runtime environment responsible for executing Java bytecode. The JVM loads classes, verifies bytecode, manages runtime memory, executes instructions, and provides services such as garbage collection.

Modern JVM implementations can also use Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation. Frequently executed bytecode can be compiled into native machine instructions at runtime, which can improve execution performance.

sections.title: What is JRE?
sections.content:
JRE stands for Java Runtime Environment. It provides the components required to run Java applications, including the JVM and the Java runtime libraries needed by those applications.

The JRE concept is useful for understanding the separation between running Java software and developing Java software. Development requires additional tools provided by the JDK.

sections.title: What is JDK?
sections.content:
JDK stands for Java Development Kit. It provides the tools required to develop Java applications as well as the components required to run them. Development tools include the Java compiler and other utilities used during development, packaging, documentation, and diagnostics.

Conceptually, the JDK provides the development environment while also containing the runtime components needed to execute Java programs.

sections.title: JDK, JRE and JVM relationship
sections.content:
The three concepts can be understood as layers of the Java environment. The JVM is responsible for executing bytecode. The runtime environment provides the JVM and runtime libraries needed by Java applications. The JDK adds development tools on top of the runtime environment.

A simplified conceptual relationship is:

JDK → Development Tools + Runtime Environment
Runtime Environment → JVM + Runtime Libraries
JVM → Executes Bytecode

topics.shortDescription: Understand JVM, JRE, and JDK and how they work together to develop and run Java applications.

topics.title: Java Compilation and Execution
topics.description: Follow the complete journey of a Java program from source code through compilation, bytecode generation, class loading, and execution by the JVM.

sections.title: Java source code
sections.content:
Java programs are normally written in source files with the `.java` extension. The source code contains classes, interfaces, methods, fields, and other language constructs that are understandable to developers.

For example, a simple Java application can contain a class with a `main` method that starts application execution.

sections.title: Compilation with javac
sections.content:
The Java compiler, commonly invoked using `javac`, converts valid Java source code into JVM bytecode. For example, compiling `HelloWorld.java` produces a class file containing compiled bytecode.

The compiler performs syntax and type checking during compilation. If the source code contains compilation errors, the compiler reports them instead of producing a valid class file for that code.

sections.title: Bytecode
sections.content:
Bytecode is the intermediate instruction format generated by the Java compiler. It is stored in class files and is designed to be executed by the JVM.

Bytecode is not the same as native machine code for a particular CPU. This distinction allows Java applications to use the same compiled representation across platforms that provide compatible JVM implementations.

sections.title: JVM execution
sections.content:
When a Java application starts, the JVM loads the required classes and executes their bytecode. The runtime can interpret bytecode and may use JIT compilation to compile frequently executed code into native instructions.

The simplified flow is:

`.java` source → Java compiler → `.class` bytecode → JVM → execution.

topics.shortDescription: Understand how Java source code is compiled into bytecode and executed by the JVM.

topics.title: Variables and Data Types

sections.title: What is a variable?
sections.content:
A variable is a named program element used to hold a value or, for a reference type, a reference to an object. Every variable has a declared type that determines which values can be assigned to it.

For example:

```java
int age = 25;
String name = "John";
```

Here, `age` is an integer variable and `name` is a reference variable referring to a String object.

topics.title: Type Casting
topics.description: Understand how Java converts values between compatible types, including widening conversions, narrowing conversions, and potential loss of information.

sections.title: Widening conversions
sections.content:
A widening numeric conversion converts a value to a type that can represent a broader range of values. Java can perform many widening primitive conversions automatically.

For example:

```java
int number = 100;
long value = number;
```

The `int` value can be assigned to a `long` without an explicit cast because the destination type has sufficient range to represent every `int` value.

topics.title: Operators
topics.description: Learn the operators Java provides for arithmetic, comparison, logical operations, assignments, bit manipulation, and conditional expressions.

sections.title: Arithmetic and assignment operators
Relational and logical operators
sections.content:
Relational operators compare values and produce boolean results. They include `==`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, and `<=`.

Logical operators combine or negate boolean expressions. Java provides `&&`, `||`, and `!` for logical operations.

The `&&` and `||` operators use short-circuit evaluation, meaning the right-hand operand may not be evaluated when the result is already determined by the left-hand operand.

sections.title: Unary and conditional operators
sections.content:
Unary operators operate on a single operand. Common examples include increment `++`, decrement `--`, unary plus `+`, unary minus `-`, and logical negation `!`.

Java also provides the conditional or ternary operator:

```java
String result = age >= 18 ? "Adult" : "Minor";
```

It evaluates a boolean condition and selects one of two expressions.

sections.title: Bitwise operators
sections.content:
Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of integral values. Java provides `&`, `|`, `^`, and `~`, along with shift operators such as `<<`, `>>`, and `>>>`.

For boolean operands, `&`, `|`, and `^` can also perform non-short-circuit logical operations. This differs from `&&` and `||`, which are conditional logical operators.

topics.shortDescription: Understand Java arithmetic, logical, relational, assignment, unary, conditional, and bitwise operators.

sections.title: What is String?
sections.content:
String is a final Java class used to represent sequences of characters. String objects are immutable, meaning their contents cannot be changed after the object has been created.

```java
String name = "Java";
```

String provides methods for operations such as comparison, searching, extracting substrings, replacing text, splitting, and converting case.

sections.title: What is a method?
Parameters and return values
sections.content:
Parameters allow a method to receive input from its caller. The return type specifies the type of value a method returns. A method declared with `void` does not return a value.

```java
int result = add(10, 20);
```

Here, `10` and `20` are arguments passed to the method, and the returned integer is assigned to `result`.


topics.title: Exception Handling Basics
topics.description: Understand exceptions in Java, the exception hierarchy, try-catch-finally, checked and unchecked exceptions, and throw and throws.

sections.title: What is an exception?
sections.content:
An exception is an object representing an abnormal condition or event that can disrupt the normal flow of program execution. Java provides a structured mechanism for detecting, propagating, and handling exceptions.

Exceptions are part of Java's throwable hierarchy. `Exception` represents conditions that applications may commonly handle, while `Error` represents serious problems generally not intended to be handled by ordinary application logic.

sections.title: try and catch
finally
Checked and unchecked exceptions
sections.content:
Checked exceptions are exceptions that the compiler requires a method to catch or declare, with the important exception that RuntimeException subclasses and Error subclasses are unchecked. Examples of checked exceptions include IOException and SQLException. Examples of unchecked exceptions include NullPointerException and IllegalArgumentException.

The distinction affects how a method's exception behavior is represented in its declaration and how callers must satisfy the compiler's exception checking rules.

topics.title: Garbage Collection Basics
topics.description: Understand Java's automatic memory management, object reachability, garbage-collection eligibility, and the role of the JVM in reclaiming heap memory.

sections.title: What is garbage collection?
sections.content:
Garbage collection is the JVM's automatic mechanism for reclaiming heap memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from the application's live references. Developers do not normally explicitly free Java objects using a manual memory-release operation.

For example:

```java
Employee employee = new Employee();
employee = null;
```

If there are no other reachable references to the Employee object, that object can become eligible for garbage collection.

sections.title: Object reachability
sections.content:
Garbage collection is based on object reachability rather than simply whether a variable contains null. An object is generally eligible for collection when it is no longer reachable from the set of GC roots through references.

An object can therefore become unreachable even when it was originally referenced by another object that itself is no longer reachable.

sections.title: Garbage collection eligibility
sections.content:
An object becoming eligible for garbage collection does not mean that the JVM will immediately reclaim its memory. The JVM and its selected garbage collector determine when collection occurs.

Applications should therefore not depend on a particular garbage-collection timing. `System.gc()` is only a request or hint to the JVM and does not guarantee that garbage collection will immediately occur.

topics.shortDescription: Understand Java garbage collection, object reachability, and automatic heap memory management.

modules.title: Control Flow
modules.description: Conditional logic, loops, and branching statements used to control the execution path of a Java program.

topics.title: Conditional Statements
topics.description: Learn how Java makes decisions using if, if-else, else-if, nested conditions, and switch statements, including traditional switch behavior and modern switch expressions.

sections.title: What conditional control flow means
sections.content:
Conditional statements allow a Java program to choose which code should execute based on a boolean condition or the value of an expression. Without conditional logic, a program would mostly execute the same sequence of statements regardless of its input.

Java provides `if`, `if-else`, `else-if`, and `switch` for making decisions. The important idea is that the condition is evaluated first, and the result determines which execution path is taken. Conditions can involve comparisons, boolean variables, method calls, or combinations of expressions using logical operators.

For example, an application might check whether a user is authenticated before allowing access to a resource, or check an order amount before applying a discount. The condition represents the decision, while the selected block represents the behavior that should follow from that decision.

topics.title: Loops
topics.description: Learn how Java repeatedly executes code using for, enhanced for, while, and do-while loops, including nested loops and the differences between pre-condition and post-condition loops.

sections.title: Why loops are needed
sections.content:
Loops allow a program to execute the same block of logic repeatedly without writing the same statements again and again. They are useful for processing collections, reading input until a condition changes, calculating repeated values, and working through arrays or other data structures.

Java provides several loop forms. A traditional `for` loop is useful when initialization, a condition, and an update are clearly defined. The enhanced `for` loop is convenient when simply visiting each element of an array or Iterable. A `while` loop is useful when repetition depends primarily on a condition, while `do-while` guarantees that the body executes at least once.

sections.title: for loop
Enhanced for loop
while loop
do-while loop
Nested loops
Choosing between loop types
sections.content:
The choice of loop should match the way the repetition is expressed. A `for` loop is natural when the loop has a counter or a clearly defined initialization and update. An enhanced `for` loop is convenient when each element simply needs to be visited. A `while` loop is appropriate when the continuation condition is the main concern and the number of iterations may not be known. A `do-while` loop is useful when the body must execute at least once.

The important distinction is not that one loop is universally faster than another. In normal Java application code, the clarity of the loop's intent is usually more important than choosing a particular loop keyword for performance reasons.

topics.shortDescription: Java loops allow code to execute repeatedly. Learn traditional for loops, enhanced for-each loops, while, do-while, nested loops, and how to choose the loop structure that matches the problem.

modules.title: OOP Fundamentals
modules.description: Object-oriented building blocks in Java, including classes, objects, constructors, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, method overloading, static members, final members, and access control.

topics.title: Object-Oriented Programming Basics
topics.description: Understand the core ideas behind object-oriented programming in Java and how encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism are represented in real Java code.

sections.title: What object-oriented programming means
sections.content:
Object-oriented programming organizes software around objects that combine state and behavior. Instead of treating a program only as a sequence of operations, OOP allows related data and the operations that work with that data to be modeled together.

Java is a class-based object-oriented language. A class defines a type, while objects are runtime instances of that type. For example, a `BankAccount` class might contain account-related state and methods such as `deposit()` and `withdraw()`.

The goal of OOP is not simply to create a large number of classes. Good object-oriented design is mainly about assigning responsibilities clearly, protecting important state, and defining useful boundaries between different parts of an application.

sections.title: The four core OOP concepts
sections.content:
The four concepts commonly associated with OOP are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism.

**Encapsulation** means keeping related state and behavior together while controlling how that state can be accessed or changed. Java commonly uses private fields and public or protected methods to achieve this.

**Abstraction** means exposing the behavior that callers need while hiding unnecessary implementation details. Java interfaces and abstract classes are common tools for defining abstractions.

**Inheritance** allows one class to derive from another class using `extends`. A subclass inherits accessible behavior from its superclass and can add or override behavior.

**Polymorphism** allows code to work with a general type while the actual implementation can vary. Method overriding is the main runtime polymorphism mechanism in Java.

Abstraction

topics.description: Learn how Java classes define types and how objects are created and used at runtime, including instance state, references, identity, and object initialization.

sections.title: Class and object relationship
Instance fields and methods
Object references
Object identity
Object creation and initialization
sections.content:
Creating an object involves several initialization steps. Memory for the object is allocated, instance fields receive their default values, instance initialization is performed, and the appropriate constructor executes.

For a class hierarchy, superclass initialization occurs before subclass-specific initialization. This ordering is important because a subclass object contains both the superclass and subclass portions of the object.

Calling an overridable instance method from a constructor can be dangerous because dynamic dispatch may invoke a subclass override before the subclass's own initialization has completed. Constructors should generally establish object state rather than rely on subclass behavior.

topics.shortDescription: A class defines a Java type while an object is a runtime instance of that type. Learn instance state, references, identity, object creation, and initialization behavior.

topics.title: Constructors
topics.description: Learn how constructors establish the initial state of objects, including overloaded constructors, constructor chaining, implicit super calls, initialization order, and validation.

sections.title: What a constructor is
Default constructor
Constructor overloading
this() constructor chaining
super() constructor chaining
Constructor initialization order
sections.content:
When an object of a subclass is created, superclass initialization happens before the subclass's initialization. The object must first establish the superclass portion before the subclass-specific initialization can complete.

This is one reason constructor behavior can become surprising in inheritance hierarchies. If a superclass constructor calls an overridable method, the subclass implementation can execute before the subclass's instance fields and initialization blocks have finished.

For this reason, constructors should generally avoid calling methods that subclasses are expected to override.

sections.title: Constructor validation

topics.shortDescription: Constructors establish the initial state of Java objects. Learn default and overloaded constructors, this() and super() chaining, initialization order, and constructor validation.

topics.title: Final Variables and Methods
topics.description: Learn how final behaves when applied to variables, references, methods, and classes, including initialization rules and the important distinction between final references and immutable objects.

sections.title: final variables
final references and mutability
sections.content:
When `final` is applied to an object reference, it prevents the reference from being changed. It does not automatically make the referenced object immutable.

```java
final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

names.add("Amit"); // valid

// names = new ArrayList<>(); // compile-time error
```

The reference must continue pointing to the same list, but the list itself can still change because `ArrayList` is mutable.

This distinction is important: `final` controls reassignment of the variable; immutability controls whether the object's observable state can change.

final classes
final fields and object initialization

topics.shortDescription: The final modifier prevents reassignment, overriding, or inheritance depending on where it is applied. Learn final variables, references, methods, classes, and initialization rules.

topics.title: Access Modifiers
topics.description: Learn Java's private, package-private, protected, and public visibility rules and how access control supports encapsulation and API design.

sections.title: The four access levels
sections.content:
Java provides four levels of member access: `private`, package-private, `protected`, and `public`.

`private` restricts access to the declaring class. Package-private access applies when no access modifier is written and allows access from classes in the same package. `protected` provides package access plus additional access for subclasses under Java's inheritance rules. `public` provides the broadest normal visibility.

Access modifiers are not merely syntax. They define which parts of a class become available to other code and therefore form part of the class's API and encapsulation boundary.

protected

modules.title: Exception Handling
modules.description: Handling exceptional situations in Java using try-catch-finally, throw, throws, custom exceptions, exception propagation, and exception hierarchy.

topics.title: Exception Handling Basics
topics.description: Understand what exceptions are, why Java uses them, how the exception hierarchy works, and how exceptions differ from normal program errors.

sections.title: What is an exception?
sections.content:
An exception represents an abnormal condition that interrupts the normal flow of a Java program. It can occur because of invalid input, a missing file, a failed network operation, an invalid array index, or many other situations.

For example:

```java
int result = 10 / 0;
```

This causes an `ArithmeticException` because integer division by zero is not valid. Instead of continuing normally, Java creates an exception object and transfers control toward exception-handling code if appropriate handling is available.

Exception handling allows an application to respond to such conditions instead of allowing an unexpected failure to terminate the current operation without explanation.

sections.title: Exception hierarchy
sections.content:
Java exceptions are organized into a class hierarchy rooted at `Throwable`. The two major branches below `Throwable` are `Error` and `Exception`.

`Error` represents serious conditions that applications generally do not attempt to recover from, such as `OutOfMemoryError` or `StackOverflowError`.

`Exception` represents conditions that application code may be able to handle. `RuntimeException` is a major subclass of `Exception` and includes exceptions such as `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, and `IndexOutOfBoundsException`.

The hierarchy matters because catching a superclass can also catch instances of its subclasses. For example, catching `Exception` can catch many different exception types, while catching `IOException` handles only that specific type and its subclasses.

Checked and unchecked exceptions

topics.title: Custom Exceptions
topics.description: Learn how to create application-specific exception types that represent meaningful business or domain failures.

sections.title: Why custom exceptions are useful
sections.content:
Standard Java exceptions describe common programming and runtime problems, but applications often have domain-specific failures that deserve clearer names.

For example, a banking application might need an `InsufficientBalanceException`, while an authentication service might use `InvalidTokenException`.

A custom exception gives the failure a meaningful type that callers can catch independently from unrelated failures. This makes exception handling more expressive and keeps business rules separate from generic runtime exceptions.

topics.title: Try-With-Resources
topics.description: Learn how Java automatically closes resources that implement AutoCloseable and how suppressed exceptions are handled during resource cleanup.

sections.title: Why resource cleanup matters
sections.content:
Resources such as files, database connections, streams, and sockets often need to be closed after use. Forgetting to close them can cause resource leaks, exhausted connection pools, open file handles, or other operational problems.

Traditional try-finally code can perform cleanup, but it becomes difficult to write correctly when multiple resources are involved or when both the main operation and cleanup can throw exceptions.

Try-with-resources provides a language feature specifically designed for this problem.

topics.title: Exception Handling Design
topics.description: Learn how to design exception handling that preserves useful context, avoids hiding failures, and places recovery decisions at the appropriate application layer.

sections.title: Catch exceptions you can handle
Preserve the original cause
Do not swallow exceptions
Do not use exceptions for ordinary control flow
sections.content:
Exceptions are designed for exceptional conditions, not as a replacement for normal conditional logic.

For example, code should not deliberately trigger an exception every time it needs to determine whether a value exists when a normal condition or API operation can express that decision clearly.

Using exceptions for expected high-frequency branches can make the code harder to understand and may introduce unnecessary overhead. Exceptions should communicate failures or exceptional situations that are meaningfully different from normal successful execution.

sections.title: Logging exception information

topics.shortDescription: Design exception handling around meaningful recovery decisions, preserved causes, useful diagnostics, and clear separation between normal control flow and exceptional failures.
